chapters.headline: THE DESERTED WIFE
chapters.text:
First up — Page 1, Column 1. THE DESERTED WIFE. BY JAMES G. PERCIVAL.
He comes not -- I have watch'd the moon go down. But yet he comes not. Once it was not so. The speaker watches an infant, remembers a husband who once loved her, and cannot hate him though he now wears a frown and "feeds his passion on a wanton's lip." Closing promise: if sickness come, she would with kindness all her wrongs repay, until the penitent should weep and say how injured and how faithful she had been.

chapters.headline: OUR FLAG IS THERE
chapters.text: OUR FLAG IS THERE. Our Flag is there! Our Flag is there! We'll hail it with three loud huzzas! Nor foeman dare to touch its hallowed stripes and stars. Ten thousand blades; Freedom's sons; "Let Democrats in might arise / Its banner'd folds of stars to guard." Later stanzas: Glory's grave; Ocean's glory wave; Democracy's victorious band. Refrain: Our flag is there, &c.

chapters.headline: Eloquence & Humor of Patrick Henry
chapters.text: Eloquence & Humor of Patrick Henry. Hook, a Scotchman of wealth suspected of being unfriendly to the American cause. During the 1781 invasion of Cornwallis and Phillips, a commissary (Venable) took two of Hook's steers. After peace Hook, on the advice of Mr. Cowan, brought trespass in the district court of New London. Henry appeared for the defendant; the clerk Jemmy Steptoe rolled on the grass with laughter; Hook cried "Beef! Beef! Beef!" The jury found for the defendant; Hook fled from talk of tar and feathers.

chapters.headline: FRENCH COURTSHIPS
chapters.text: FRENCH COURTSHIPS. Parents of a son of one-and-twenty or two-and-twenty and parents of a younger daughter name the portion each will give; a friend matches the sums; the young persons meet at a friend's house to see how they like each other; a few formal visits in the presence of the mother; marriage in a few weeks. From Paris and its people.

chapters.headline: Treatment of Napoleon at St. Helena
chapters.text:
Treatment of Napoleon at St. Helena. Mrs. Abell's recollections: a damped piano; Mr. Guinness, band master on the General Kidd, stopped by the Governor from coming ashore to tune it; a boa constrictor brought by Sir Murray Maxwell; Napoleon's wish to see it not complied with.
Short fillers: the Amistad case revived (Spanish minister claims $40,000); anecdote of Tom Steele the Repealer and the Attorney General ("I'll strike you out of this indictment"); Choice Sayings; leap-year editor of the Tennessee Herald and Miss Lydia Green (his gray horse and patent lever); an elephant in Whitby, England, drinking porter; A Bank of $50,000,000 (Hartford Times on Clay's project); Bonaparte an awkward dancer; monument to Jackson at Baltimore; a Portland minister; a silver plate dated 1681 at Green Bay; Boston cotton goods to China; education in Russia; "Coming to the Point"; Senator Benton still kept from the Senate after the Princeton explosion.

chapters.headline: AN ACT TO REGULATE THE MILITIA
chapters.text: AN ACT TO REGULATE THE MILITIA. Training of rank and file dispensed with in time of peace except as provided. Every able-bodied white male inhabitant 21 to 45 enrolled, except volunteer companies, persons absolutely exempted, idiots, and lunatics. Township assessors to list persons liable; tavern-keepers and householders to give names; $5 fine for refusal or false information, to common schools. Enrollment roll to the township clerk, copy in May or June to the commandant of brigade. Option: volunteer company, or fifty cents commutation, or two days' extra road labor. Assessor to collect the fifty cents by distress after August 1 unless a volunteer, fire/hose/hook-and-ladder, or road-work certificate is shown. Moneys to the county treasurer as a brigade military fund. Assessor pay as for tax assessment, from the military fund. Treasurer pays on order of the commandant of brigade; two per cent. On actual service, organize as now required; present brigade and division boundaries continue. Former commissioned officers exempt from the commutation. Civil officers who neglect forfeit $20 to $100.

Next up — Page 1, Columns 5-6. GATHERINGS AND GOSSIPPINGS. "A snapper up of unconsidered trifles." First court in the territory now Ohio opened at Marietta (Campus Martius), 2 September 1788, Rufus Putnam presiding. London Globe on foreign grain; empire of woman; Mrs. Gaines's New Orleans suit $15,000,000; a Whig paper on the one thing that can prevent Clay's election (Van Buren); seven / eight / ten hours' sleep; Maryland debt over twelve millions; Michigan emigration 20,000; President Tyler $200 to the mother of his black servant killed on the Princeton; a good farmer; Whitefield on a long prayer; J. I. Codington Democratic candidate for Mayor in New York; common salt for snake bite; Mrs. Earger of Petersville, 4 children at a birth; a young lawyer and Miss Benedict of Tarrytown; Liverpool cellar-dwellers; flour from Lakes Michigan and Erie; Cleveland Whig log cabin ("Walk up to the bar and LIQUOR"); Philadelphia real estate $98,833,274; Plainfield Bank inquiry, New Jersey; Ohio second wool-growing State; London to Bristol in ninety minutes; death of Fairfield the poet; King of the Belgians' ball; Maryland legislature adjourned without interest provision; bustles / romances; General Hamilton of South Carolina for Clay; tax on new-ship materials; Eugene Sue, *Le Juif Errant*; T. W. Gilmer left $430,000, Judge Upshur $70,000; rewards of merit; "hen fruit"; Mrs. John Sewall of Henry County, Kentucky, two noble sons and a daughter at one birth.

chapters.headline: ALCIBIADES AND CLAY
chapters.text: ALCIBIADES AND CLAY. Alcibiades all things to all men (Sparta, Ionia, Thrace, Tissaphernes). Clay in the West the friend of the farmer and log cabins; in the North and East for a high Protective Tariff; in the South a free-trade man. Speaker Polk; brag with Lord Ashburton; moderator at a religious discussion in Kentucky; Jackson denounced, then the 8th of January celebrated at New Orleans; once opposed a United States bank, now a National Bank of fifty millions. "Farmer of Ashland," "Mill boy of the Slashes," Durham cattle.

chapters.headline: CANDIDATES
chapters.text:
CANDIDATES. The following publication by the Democratic Central Committee of this County will explain itself. No returns have been received from some of the Townships; and whether they have voted or not, we are not advised. The names mentioned in the following publication will compose the ticket, unless other returns are received to change the result.
The undersigned members of the Democratic Central Committee of Harrison county, Ohio, do hereby certify the following to be the result of the election, under the popular vote system held on the first day of April instant, for the purpose of electing or nominating candidates for State and County officers, at the coming election in 1844, in said Harrison county, to wit:
Among the several candidates for Representative
Charles Warfel had 123 maj.
For Commissioner, David Finicum had 65 "
For Recorder, Matthew M. Sloan had 607 "

chapters.headline: Page 2, Columns 2-4
chapters.text:
Next up — Page 2, Columns 2-4. Page 2, Columns 2-4. The Late War -- Federal Misrepresentation Exposed -- base Falsehoods nailed to the counter -- Facts taken from History -- Read and Circulate.
Albany Daily Citizen and the KAY-diz Whig Standard charged that Van Buren opposed the war of 1812. The Sentinel answers from the record: Hudson meeting, 31 January 1809 (Jefferson still President); resolutions of 1810 for Madison, Tompkins, and Broome; April 1811 Hudson resolutions; April 1812 election to the New York Senate; Clinton nomination as the regular Republican ticket; June 1812 war declared; November 1812 reply to the Governor sustaining the war; March 1813 navy report and $500,000 loan; 9 March 1813 address ("WAR, AND WAR ALONE"); 1813-14 defender of Tompkins; 14 April 1814 Albany meeting; extra session 1814, 12,000-man act drawn by Van Buren; February 1815 resolutions of thanks to Jackson and New Orleans; $350,000 loan to pay militia; Attorney General. Col. Stone of the Commercial Advertiser allowed as an honest opponent. Close: preserve this paper.

chapters.headline: HOW STANDS THE UNION!
chapters.text:
Next up — Page 2, Columns 5-6. HOW STANDS THE UNION!. State-by-state contrast of 1840 and 1844 (New York, Pennsylvania, Maine, Indiana, Michigan, New Jersey, Mississippi, Ohio, Connecticut, Louisiana, Georgia, North Carolina, Kentucky, Tennessee, Rhode Island, Vermont, Wisconsin). chapters.text: LOOK UPON THIS PICTURE. Aliases of the opponents of democracy, numbered 1-33 (Federalists through the Mill Boy of the Slashes and Cologne Party). A man known in one section as Smith, in another as Brown, in another as Scroggins -- not a local surname notice. Oily Gammon on denial. Southern Clay papers (Richmond Whig, Mobile Tribune, N. Orleans Bee) claim him more of a free-trade man than Van Buren. Will a federal sheet in this Congressional District dare publish Clay's letter to Dr. Bronson?

chapters.headline: PROVIDENTIAL DISPENSATIONS

Hornby knocked down Mr. D. H. Twogood and stamped him to death; the meeting went on. Clay at a Sabbath military parade in New Orleans and a Sabbath arrival at Mobile. Crush of the Clay club-house at Richmond. Warning against a similar mode of electioneering.
Fillers: jail at Somerset, Perry Co., Ohio, burnt; Nichols Higgin escaped. Governor of Mississippi, $2000 for Richard S. Graves, defaulting State Treasurer. Calico printed in this country. The Hon. Heman A. Moore, M. C., from the Columbus district, is dead. (ALTO of the given name is "Neman"; page-image crop was read as Heman.)

chapters.headline: Base Forgery
chapters.text:
Base Forgery. Federal papers publishing a Clay eulogy said to be by the Rev. Wm. Capers; Capers denies it.
Calhoun arrived at Washington as Secretary of State. Hayti disturbances. Dr. Hubbard has resigned as Fund Commissioner; Gov. Shannon has appointed Joseph S. Lake. Jackson letter to Santa Anna on Texan prisoners. Maine legislature; Texas-annexation instructions failed. Theophilus Fenn of the Harrisburgh Telegraph eloped. Presbyterian General Assembly, Louisville, 16 May. Walworth and Shannon nominations lying on the Senate table. Straps to pants going out.

Presbyterian General Assembly, Louisville, 16 May. Walworth and Shannon nominations lying on the Senate table. Straps to pants going out.
